The Isle of Man: More Than Just the TT

The Isle of Man is famous for the TT races, but it offers far more than two weeks of racing action. This self-governing Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea has Viking history, stunning mountain roads, beautiful beaches, and — crucially for motorcyclists — no national speed limit on many derestricted roads. It's a motorcycle-friendly island year-round.

The Mountain Road

The Mountain Road from Ramsey to Douglas is the most spectacular section of the TT course and equally thrilling at road speed. Climbing to 422 metres, it crosses open moorland with views across the entire island. On clear days, you can see Scotland, England, Ireland, and Wales simultaneously. The road is derestricted (no speed limit) outside race periods — ride responsibly and within your abilities.

Beyond the TT Course

The island has a comprehensive road network offering varied riding:

  • The Coastal Road — A complete loop of the island takes about 3 hours and covers 100 miles of stunning coastline
  • The Millennium Way — Heritage trail from Castletown to Ramsey through the island's interior
  • Marine Drive — Dramatic cliff-top road between Douglas and Port Soderick
  • Calf of Man — View this uninhabited island from the southern tip at Cregneash

Viking and Celtic Heritage

The Isle of Man has a rich Norse heritage. Tynwald, the island's parliament, has met continuously since 979 AD — making it one of the world's oldest continuous parliaments. The Manx Museum in Douglas tells the story of the island from prehistoric to modern times. Castle Rushen in Castletown is a beautifully preserved medieval fortress. Peel Castle on its island promontory is atmospheric and photogenic.

Visit the Isle of Man outside TT fortnight and you'll find a peaceful, beautiful island with empty roads and a genuine motorcycle-friendly culture that extends year-round.

When to Visit

TT fortnight (late May/early June) is the island's marquee event — the atmosphere is electric but accommodation prices triple and the course is closed for practice and racing. The Manx Grand Prix (late August) is a smaller, more accessible racing event. For riding the roads at your own pace, visit in April-May or September-October when the weather is reasonable and the roads are quiet.

Practical Information

The Isle of Man Steam Packet operates ferries from Heysham (3.5 hours), Liverpool (2.5 hours by fast craft), and Belfast. Book motorcycle spaces well in advance for TT period — they sell out months ahead. The island has fuel stations in every town. The Manx Pound is interchangeable with Sterling. Mobile coverage is good across most of the island.

The Derestricted Roads

Many Manx roads have no speed limit on derestricted sections (marked by the national speed limit sign). This doesn't mean these roads are safe to ride flat out — they're regular public roads with junctions, pedestrians, and oncoming traffic. The derestricted policy reflects the island's motorcycle-friendly culture, not an invitation to race. Ride within your abilities and respect other road users.
